Lab grown meat

By: Eugene Botha | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
....we taste a burger made from lab grown meat

Unique Selling Point:
New technology -- cellular agriculture

Summary:
Lab grown meat or cultured meat will soon be available in South African supermarkets through a South African start-up called Mzansi Meat Co. And apparently, the product is quite tasty!

Further information:
About six years ago I did a story on meat grown in a lab in the Netherlands. It was quite futuristic and revolutionary at the time it cost $250 000 to created. All in all, it seemed to be more in the realm of science fiction be quite far removed from us here in Africa.

However, lab grown meat or cultured meat will soon be available in South African supermarkets through a South African start-up called Mzansi Meat Co.

And apparently the product is quite tasty!


This ground-breaking start-up was founded by Brett Thompson and Tasneem Karodia.

They say:
“We’ve always had a thing for meat. It’s easy to see why – meat goes with all occasions and brings us together to make moments more flavourful. It’s also a rich form of protein loved by cultures the world over. The journey from the source to our plate however, comes at a cost. That’s where Mzansi Meat Co. was born – out of a relentless pursuit to reimagine our food systems and the way we make meat. We’re bringing healthy, accessible and affordable meat to your braais, potjies and shisa nyamas by growing it from cells, without harming animals.”

And it is not idle talk. They have produced Africa’s first cultivated beef burger, and it was unveiled at an event in April 2022.

At the moment production is at a small scale but in the coming years, Mzansi plans to open a pilot plant and develop more products such as cultivated nuggets, sausages, and steaks.

The meat alternatives will be tailored to the African market, helping to sustainably feed a growing population. A study last year found that 60% of South Africans would be willing to try cultivated meat, a much higher figure than in many Western countries.

The process they developed to cultivate meat in the lab is different from many other approaches in the sense that they do not start out with animal stems cells, but actual animal cells. It begins with a visit to a local farm animal sanctuary where donor animals are living their best life, in peace.

A registered state veterinarian removes tiny tissue cells from the animal with as little harm as possible.

Once the cells are harvested, a sample is placed in a nutrient-rich transport medium and taken to the lab where we isolate the cells and grow them in a culture medium. This is a special type of food containing vitamins, salts and proteins that the cells need to develop and divide. Once there are enough cells, they are placed on an edible structure and after adding a few additional spices and flavours, the meat is ready to be dished up and enjoyed.

See also https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0a_f4UuqjLA&t=63s
In May they also presented their first cultured beef burger to the world at a major international conference in Switzerland.

It is an innovative, young company with a sense of humour and is indeed part of innovations that are already beginning to transform the food industry.
For the story we will visit their headquarters in Cape Town, visit the animal sanctuary to see how the biopsies are done, visit the lab when the meat is grown, and we will cook and taste the burgers.

THE BROADER CONTEXT
Lab grown meat falls within the broader field of cellular agriculture where cells and not animals are used to grow large quantities of food, including meat.
Cultured meat has been called many different names in its short lifespan, including clean, synthetic, and lab-grown meat. No matter the label, they all refer to the same thing, essentially a product that’s been grown from the cells of animals. Cultured meat is produced from animal cells that propagate in a medium in which they can grow to an abundance that they create enough ‘meat’ for people to eat.
Traditional animal agriculture has many downsides and has a huge influence of the environment:
• It is estimated that globally 80 billion animals (domestic livestock) are killed each year for food. Sometimes in extremely inhumane conditions.

• Livestock is the largest user of land resources. It is estimated that permanent meadows and pastures accounted for 26 per cent of the global land area. Between 33 and 40 per cent of global arable land is used to grow feed crops. Together, permanent meadows, pastures and land dedicated to the production of feed thus represent 80 per cent of total agricultural land. And 30% of the world’s freshwater supply is used in the process.

• Animal agriculture is responsible for an estimated 14.5 percent of manmade carbon emissions that contribute to climate change each year (and perhaps up to 25 percent by some estimates), making raising animals more deleterious to our planet's health than the combined transportation sector altogether.

• Additionally, animal agriculture is contributing to polluting waterways, as run-off from concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) makes its way into the watershed. When thousands of animals live in small, confined areas, their waste washes into neighbouring streams, rivers, and oceans, where dead zones form.

Many say the advent of lab grown meat is inevitable for the following reasons:
• No animals are harmed in the process of developing lab-grown meat. All one needs is to harmlessly extract muscle tissue from an animal, which can then be used to produce meat through the cultivation of cells.

• The European Environment Agency suggests that cultivated meat could offer 78–96% lower greenhouse gas emissions, 99% less land use, and 82–96% less water use compared to conventionally produced meat.

• Lab-grown meat also provides benefits for human health. Farm animals are fed large quantities of antibiotics as a quick measure to prevent illnesses. As humans eat the meat of farm animals, we too needlessly consume antibiotics, which allow germs to develop a resistance to them. Lab grown meat contains no antibiotics.

• It has become economically viable. The first lab grown burger patty in 2013 cost $330 000 to create. Future Meat, accompany in Israel, has produced a chicken breast for $1.70 in 2021.

Script:


V/O:
The white coats and determined walk might give them the look of scientists, but these are farmers. Well, farmers with a twist, that is: they’re growing top quality beef. But without animals.
Brett:
So What we are doing is making a cow without the cow.
V/O:
Well, cow flesh to be specific. And if that turns you off, feast your eyes on this: a burger unlike any burger you’ve ever eaten. You see, the meat has been engineered in a process that might just change global food production forever.

Cape Town’s Mzansi Meat Company produces cultivated meat, that is, meat grown in a lab – with not an animal in sight.

Their CEO, Brett Thompson, says it heralds a more ethical food production system, with one simple aim.
Brett:
Providing meat that doesn't require an animal to be killed, but taste exactly the same. It tastes like beef, and when that is available to people, I think the world will just naturally move to a food system where we no longer need animals to be killed.
V/O:
It’s a noble ambition with one major challenge: to succeed, their lab-produced meat must taste just like the original.

Enter Absie Pantshwa: Mzansi’s Head of Taste. You might say the company’s putting it’s money where her mouth is:
Masa:
Your job title Head of Taste. Let’s talk about it. It sounds very interesting.

Absie:
So when it comes to the taste and the texture, that is where the magic lies. It is keeping us honest when it comes to the texture, the taste and to make sure everything always comes through as what it is, which is beef.
V/O:
Brett says to create perfect cultivated beef is relatively straightforward.
Brett:
It starts with a single biopsy, a tissue sample we take from a cow.It is about the size of a peppercorn and then we take that small tissue sample and bring it our facility here in Woodstock.
V/O:
Freshly harvested from cows we’re assured aren’t harmed in the process, the sample is handed to Mzansi staff who separate a few muscle and fat cells before putting them in a special growth medium in an incubator.
Brett:
And once they start growing they start duplicating and they grow and they gro and grow, and that couple of cells trun into trillions, and then turn into enough so we can harvest it.
V/O:
We’re given a tour of this revolutionary ranch. There’s a general lab where the substances that’ll help the meat grow are prepared.
Brett:
And then we move in what we have called The Pasture. So the Pasture is where you can actually see our team actually isolating the cells.
V/O:
Here a few cells are put in special dishes where they begin growing and multiplying in an incubator. From just a few cells to millions.
Masa:
So where do we find ourselves now?

Brett:
This is the bioprocessing room. We also call it the Kraal.

Masa:
So this is the Kraal

Brett:
The Kraal.
V/O:
Here, millions of cells from the pasture are put into what are known as bioreactors where they multiply, forming colourless little pieces of meat.

Then the lab grown meat heads to Absie who adds colour, flavour, and texture. For a demo, she needs a freshly grown sample – and that’s in the hands of Doctor Kyle Naylor – brilliant but notoriously late.
Absie:
Here is Kyle now.

Masa:
So, please explain to us what we will be doing here. From all of this we are going to get a burger patty.

Kyle:
A burger patty, yes.
V/O:
Kyle brought just enough meat for a slider. Lab-grown meat is colourless, so he mixes in the special ingredients prepared by Absie, adds a little water and some coconut oil and… there it is: lab grown meat transformed into something resembling ground beef.

It was left to me to turn it into a patty.
UP SOUND:
…. Viola…. Food scientist…… that is a cultivated beef patty.
V/O:
In April this year, Mzansi unveiled Africa’s first cultivated beef patty at a gala function in Cape Town. Tasneem Karodia, is Co-Founder and farm manager.
Masa:
Tasneem, how expensive is this meat?

Tasneem:
In 2013, the first burger that was made in the Netherlands was $250 000. We are excited to say that the cost has come down dramatically. In April one of the burgers we had at our event cost R20 000.
V/O:
And, if you’re wondering, the burger we just created cost around R3000. But the company is aiming for a product that costs no more than conventional meat.

Until then, let’s see how our 3 grand version delivers on taste…
Masa:
Well, if you want to prepare a very special burger, you need a special kitchen right? And what is better than the Master Chef kitchen?
V/O:
A unique tasting awaited.
Masa:
Is this for me?

Absie:
Yes.
Will you do us the honours.

UPSOUND
……….feels special….. there’s that nice sizzle.
V/O:
Within minutes thepatty was ready to become the centrepiece of a truly cutting-edge burger.
UPSOUND
………….right.
V/O
With some slap chips as a side, this was the fruit of our labour: from Petrie dish to plate, a fully-fledged lab grown burger.
Masa:
Are their other companies in South Africa doing this?

Brett:
When we started there was not a single cultivated meat company in Africa. Anow we see a couple more happening, just the last two years. So there is a company in Johannesburg that is doing venison, and thye have also managed to cultivate chicken. And there is also a company that is doing fish. It is exciting, it means that it is an industry that is growing, and we are really passionate about it and cannot wait to take what we are doing to the rest of Africa.
Voce:
So, with a continent waiting, what of other types of meat?
Tasneem:
Absolutely. We have already started to look at other species so we ‘ve got pig and chicken and lamb as well.

Masa:
So in the future one day we can look forward to some good pork ribs, made in the lab.

Tasneem:
Absolutely.

Masa:
Tasting just as good?

Tasneem:
Yes, exactly the same. Just made better.


V/O
Back in the kitchen it was time to taste!
Absie:
This is the moment of truth…

Masa:
The moment of truth. It looks pretty good, it smells pretty good, but does it taste really good?
V/O:
Not one to speak with my mouth full – I let my expression do the talking. But, it was in every way, indistinguishable from regular meat.
Absie:
And how was that? Did the texture come through of a beef patty?

Masa:
Absolutely. The seasoning as well the texture, the softness. But what is even more interesting is that I am the tenth person in the universe to evert try a Mzansi Meat Company burger. I mean, more people have walked on the moon.

V/O:
From here, the plan is to ensure cultivated meat is within reach of every South African as soon as possible. If they succeed, it’ll be another step for a global movement hoping to transform how we produce our food. Ask them and they’ll tell you the future of our planet depends on it.

---------------------------------------------------
V/O:
These are the farmers of the future. They produce top quality meat, without ever setting foot on a farm.

Brett:
So What we are doing is making a cow without the cow.

--------------------------------------------------

V/O:
This hamburger is like no other burger you’ve eaten. Its central ingredient, the meat, has been re-engineered by farmers of the future.

They grow top-quality beef without ever setting foot in a field.

Brett:
So what we are doing is making a cow without the cow.

V/O:
How lab-grown meat is totally re-inventing food production.

--------------------------------------------------------------

V/O:
The meat on this juicy burger was not obtained by killing an animal. It was entirely grown in a lab, starting of with just a few beef cells placed in a lab dish where they start to duplicate and grow.

Brett:
And that couple of cells turn into their trillions until there is enough so that we can harvest it.

V/O:
Would you be willing taste the meat of the future?

V/O With some slap chips as a side, this was the fruit of our labour: from Petrie dish to plate, a fully-fledged lab grown burger. Masa: Are their other companies in South Africa doing this? Brett: When we started there was not a single cultivated meat company in Africa. Anow we see a couple more happening, just the last two years. So there is a company in Johannesburg that is doing venison, and thye have also managed to cultivate chicken. And there is also a company that is doing fish. It is exciting, it means that it is an industry that is growing, and we are really passionate about it and cannot wait to take what we are doing to the rest of Africa. Voce: So, with a continent waiting, what of other types of meat? Tasneem: Absolutely. We have already started to look at other species so we ‘ve got pig and chicken and lamb as well. Masa: So in the future one day we can look forward to some good pork ribs, made in the lab. Tasneem: Absolutely. Masa: Tasting just as good? Tasneem: Yes, exactly the same. Just made better. V/O Back in the kitchen it was time to taste! Absie: This is the moment of truth… Masa: The moment of truth. It looks pretty good, it smells pretty good, but does it taste really good? V/O: Not one to speak with my mouth full – I let my expression do the talking. But, it was in every way, indistinguishable from regular meat. Absie: And how was that? Did the texture come through of a beef patty? Masa: Absolutely. The seasoning as well the texture, the softness. But what is even more interesting is that I am the tenth person in the universe to evert try a Mzansi Meat Company burger. I mean, more people have walked on the moon. V/O: From here, the plan is to ensure cultivated meat is within reach of every South African as soon as possible. If they succeed, it’ll be another step for a global movement hoping to transform how we produce our food. Ask them and they’ll tell you the future of our planet depends on it. --------------------------------------------------- V/O: These are the farmers of the future. They produce top quality meat, without ever setting foot on a farm. Brett: So What we are doing is making a cow without the cow. -------------------------------------------------- V/O: This hamburger is like no other burger you’ve eaten. Its central ingredient, the meat, has been re-engineered by farmers of the future. They grow top-quality beef without ever setting foot in a field. Brett: So what we are doing is making a cow without the cow. V/O: How lab-grown meat is totally re-inventing food production. -------------------------------------------------------------- V/O: The meat on this juicy burger was not obtained by killing an animal. It was entirely grown in a lab, starting of with just a few beef cells placed in a lab dish where they start to duplicate and grow. Brett: And that couple of cells turn into their trillions until there is enough so that we can harvest it. V/O: Would you be willing taste the meat of the future?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ....we taste a burger made from lab grown meat
metadata.Summary: Lab grown meat or cultured meat will soon be available in South African supermarkets through a South African start-up called Mzansi Meat Co. And apparently, the product is quite tasty!
metadata.Further information: About six years ago I did a story on meat grown in a lab in the Netherlands. It was quite futuristic and revolutionary at the time it cost $250 000 to created. All in all, it seemed to be more in the realm of science fiction be quite far removed from us here in Africa. However, lab grown meat or cultured meat will soon be available in South African supermarkets through a South African start-up called Mzansi Meat Co. And apparently the product is quite tasty! This ground-breaking start-up was founded by Brett Thompson and Tasneem Karodia. They say: “We’ve always had a thing for meat. It’s easy to see why – meat goes with all occasions and brings us together to make moments more flavourful. It’s also a rich form of protein loved by cultures the world over. The journey from the source to our plate however, comes at a cost. That’s where Mzansi Meat Co. was born – out of a relentless pursuit to reimagine our food systems and the way we make meat. We’re bringing healthy, accessible and affordable meat to your braais, potjies and shisa nyamas by growing it from cells, without harming animals.” And it is not idle talk. They have produced Africa’s first cultivated beef burger, and it was unveiled at an event in April 2022. At the moment production is at a small scale but in the coming years, Mzansi plans to open a pilot plant and develop more products such as cultivated nuggets, sausages, and steaks. The meat alternatives will be tailored to the African market, helping to sustainably feed a growing population. A study last year found that 60% of South Africans would be willing to try cultivated meat, a much higher figure than in many Western countries. The process they developed to cultivate meat in the lab is different from many other approaches in the sense that they do not start out with animal stems cells, but actual animal cells. It begins with a visit to a local farm animal sanctuary where donor animals are living their best life, in peace. A registered state veterinarian removes tiny tissue cells from the animal with as little harm as possible. Once the cells are harvested, a sample is placed in a nutrient-rich transport medium and taken to the lab where we isolate the cells and grow them in a culture medium. This is a special type of food containing vitamins, salts and proteins that the cells need to develop and divide. Once there are enough cells, they are placed on an edible structure and after adding a few additional spices and flavours, the meat is ready to be dished up and enjoyed. See also https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0a_f4UuqjLA&t=63s In May they also presented their first cultured beef burger to the world at a major international conference in Switzerland. It is an innovative, young company with a sense of humour and is indeed part of innovations that are already beginning to transform the food industry. For the story we will visit their headquarters in Cape Town, visit the animal sanctuary to see how the biopsies are done, visit the lab when the meat is grown, and we will cook and taste the burgers. THE BROADER CONTEXT Lab grown meat falls within the broader field of cellular agriculture where cells and not animals are used to grow large quantities of food, including meat. Cultured meat has been called many different names in its short lifespan, including clean, synthetic, and lab-grown meat. No matter the label, they all refer to the same thing, essentially a product that’s been grown from the cells of animals. Cultured meat is produced from animal cells that propagate in a medium in which they can grow to an abundance that they create enough ‘meat’ for people to eat. Traditional animal agriculture has many downsides and has a huge influence of the environment: • It is estimated that globally 80 billion animals (domestic livestock) are killed each year for food. Sometimes in extremely inhumane conditions. • Livestock is the largest user of land resources. It is estimated that permanent meadows and pastures accounted for 26 per cent of the global land area. Between 33 and 40 per cent of global arable land is used to grow feed crops. Together, permanent meadows, pastures and land dedicated to the production of feed thus represent 80 per cent of total agricultural land. And 30% of the world’s freshwater supply is used in the process. • Animal agriculture is responsible for an estimated 14.5 percent of manmade carbon emissions that contribute to climate change each year (and perhaps up to 25 percent by some estimates), making raising animals more deleterious to our planet's health than the combined transportation sector altogether. • Additionally, animal agriculture is contributing to polluting waterways, as run-off from concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) makes its way into the watershed. When thousands of animals live in small, confined areas, their waste washes into neighbouring streams, rivers, and oceans, where dead zones form. Many say the advent of lab grown meat is inevitable for the following reasons: • No animals are harmed in the process of developing lab-grown meat. All one needs is to harmlessly extract muscle tissue from an animal, which can then be used to produce meat through the cultivation of cells. • The European Environment Agency suggests that cultivated meat could offer 78–96% lower greenhouse gas emissions, 99% less land use, and 82–96% less water use compared to conventionally produced meat. • Lab-grown meat also provides benefits for human health. Farm animals are fed large quantities of antibiotics as a quick measure to prevent illnesses. As humans eat the meat of farm animals, we too needlessly consume antibiotics, which allow germs to develop a resistance to them. Lab grown meat contains no antibiotics. • It has become economically viable. The first lab grown burger patty in 2013 cost $330 000 to create. Future Meat, accompany in Israel, has produced a chicken breast for $1.70 in 2021.
